newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Tanzania privatisation on track as revenues climb.
newsitem.headline: Tanzania privatisation on track as revenues climb.

text.p: Tanzanian authorities said on Wednesday the sale and restructuring of mostly ailing state companies was on track and had earned the government $78 million plus commitments of $101.7 million over a three-year period.

In a presentation to an international investor forum in the capital Dar es Salaam, Parastatal Sector Reform Commission chairman George Mbowa said a total of 72 sale agreements and 91 memorandums of understanding had been signed between 1992 and October 1996.
The financially ailing firms are a legacy of almost 30 years of socialist-style economic policies that ended with the 1985 retirement of first president Julius Nyerere.
The November 5-8 forum, the biggest gathering of investors in this vast East African country, was attended by 500 foreign and local business people, including 61 companies from India.
On Tuesday, Tanzania's vice-president told foreign investors his country would press ahead with economic reforms and strive to clear hurdles blocking development.
Vice-President Omar Ali Juma, in a speech read on behalf of President Benjamin Mkapa, vowed to streamline tax and investment policies and overhaul outdated immigration laws.

"The increase in scope and breadth of PSRC divestiture operations continued to be fuelled by the momentum of growth led by the new private sector and also by deterioration of the parastatals due to lack to working capital," said Mbowe.
The Commission's activities focused on a widening range of state-owned enterprises, placing priority for sales on enterprises with significant impact on the budget, he said.

The best known example of parastatal sales was that of Tanzania Breweries Ltd (TBL). South African Breweries, through its subsidiary Indol International, purchased a 50 per cent shareholding in TBL in December 1993 in a $22.5 million deal.
The result was remarkable. Since privatisation, TBL has paid dividends to the government of some 2.0 billion shillings -- the first time in 20 years of TBL history a dividend had been paid.
Annual growth in 1996 was around 44 per cent compared to nil percent in 1993 and 13 percent in 1994. TBL sales totalled 102 billion shillings in 1996 from 24.5 billion shillings in 1993.
Mbowe said one negative aspect of the sales was staff cutbacks. The government simply had no idea on what to do with those forced to retire.
But he saw grounds for optimism, citing the examples of Williamson Diamond, Tanga Cement, Tanzania Cigarette Company and Tanzania Electric Goods, where privatisation has created jobs.
